meta.source: Martens, M., De Wolf, R., Vandendriessche, K., Evens, T., & De Marez, L. (2021). Applying contextual integrity to digital contact tracing and automated triage for hospitals during COVID-19. Technology in Society, 67, 101748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techsoc.2021.101748 (open access: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8448401/)
meta.practice: Digital contact tracing during COVID-19: smartphone location/proximity data (GPS, GSM, Bluetooth) collected by government or app-developing companies and processed for pandemic-control goals of varying individual impact
meta.practice_input: During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments and companies (e.g., Google, Apple, or local developers) deploy digital contact tracing applications on citizens' smartphones. The app collects data about citizens' movements and encounters — precise GPS location, coarser GSM cell-tower location, or Bluetooth proximity signals registering nearby phones — and processes it for public-health goals: suggesting a 14-day quarantine to individuals who came into contact with an infected person, restricting individuals' access to certain locations, or estimating the spread of the virus at a societal level. Participation reaches large parts of the population, and the system partially automates decisions previously made by human contact tracers. The practice is introduced as a temporary crisis measure, but the infrastructure could persist after the pandemic. Should this practice continue as-is, be modified, or be rejected?
meta.annotator_notes: Contamination call: published 2021 (pre-cutoff) but in Technology in Society — a niche venue for CI work — by a Belgian (Ghent/imec-mict-UGent) team studying Flanders; it is one of many COVID contact-tracing privacy surveys, not a canonical or heavily-cited CI text, so contaminated=false per the prefer-obscure-venues policy; flip to true if a citation check shows it is canonical. Completeness judgments for s5 are annotator calls: means sit near the scale midpoint with large SDs (~1.4-1.5), so data-type and goal norms are coded 'contested' rather than 'entrenched' even where a mean exceeds 3; only the societal-goal norm (estimating spread, M=3.77, and d=1.62 vs the high-impact goal) approaches entrenchment but is kept 'contested' given post-pandemic decline. TP vocabulary: 'purpose' added to the working vocabulary (logged in ANNOTATION_GUIDE.md) — the source folds purpose into transmission principles ('methods and purposes'), as many empirical CI operationalizations do. The task brief called this Apthorpe-style, but the paper does not cite Apthorpe and describes itself as supplementary to vignette studies — it uses direct Likert appropriateness items, not factorial vignettes. Second-pass fields: s5 completeness codes, s4 normalization of 'goals' as purpose, contamination call.
source_deviations: The paper is an empirical measurement of CI parameters (survey, paired-sample t-tests), not a 9-step heuristic traversal; the step mapping here is annotator-imposed.

Only two CI parameters are varied and measured — information types and goals/purposes. The authors state the survey 'could not include direct questions concerning the appropriateness of actors and other transmission principles' due to length constraints; actors appear only as fixed background framing.

The paper operationalizes transmission principles loosely as 'methods and purposes' of data processing, folding purpose-of-use into the TP parameter rather than treating TPs strictly as constraints on flow.

Second strand not annotated here: automated triage for hospitals (data types: age, gender, medical self-assessment questionnaire, medical history, ICU occupancy; goals from individual care suggestions to denying hospital access to societal ICU-occupancy estimation; finding: only gender rated significantly less appropriate among data types; H1b, H2b, H3b confirmed). H4 (cross-context): comparable goals were rated differently between the contact tracing and triage contexts — evidence for context-dependence of norms, but still descriptive.

No s2 domain analysis: the health/crisis context is framed via surveillance-studies literature (dataveillance, data colonialism, panopticon) and an ADM definition, without analysis of the context's roles, activities, values, and ends.
No s6 prima facie verdict: means and hypothesis tests are reported but never converted into a violation/no-violation judgment on any specific flow.
No s7/s8: power and surveillance concerns appear in the theory section as literature framing, not as a factor-by-factor moral/political analysis of this practice.

No s9 continue/modify/reject verdict. Policy-relevant findings stop short of a decision: (a) 'transparent communication on the underlying ideas and goals is necessary when digital contact tracing and automated triage systems are rolled out'; (b) warning that temporary measures established during a crisis can become permanent and reduce citizens' privacy — the measured post-pandemic drop in appropriateness supports sunsetting; (c) citizens are willing to share personal data if they consider the specific context appropriate, so design and regulation should incorporate public expectations (citizen-centered governance) rather than assume blanket refusal or blanket acceptance.

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: goals (transmission principles as 'methods and purposes' of processing): suggesting a 14-day quarantine (low individual impact), limiting access to certain locations (high individual impact), estimating the spread of the virus (societal)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: §2.2 (CI parameters: actors, information types, and 'transmission principles (methods and purposes)'); §3.2 goal items; H2a: significant differences between goal types by impact level

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: temporal dimension of appropriateness: during vs. after the COVID-19 pandemic
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: §2.3.3 ('norms are constantly in the process of becoming'; H3a/H3b: appropriateness of data types and goals differs during versus after COVID-19); §3.2: respondents who said they would answer differently post-COVID re-answered the items hypothetically

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: decentralised privacy-preserving proximity tracing (DP3T): notifying exposed users without actually tracing social contacts
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: §2.1/§2.3.1: DP3T and the Apple/Google API offer decentralized designs that notify users of exposure 'without actually tracing social contacts' — raised as background design constraint, not empirically varied in the survey

s5_norms.norm_flow: During the pandemic, citizens' coarse or proximity-based data (GSM cell-tower location, Bluetooth encounters) may flow from their smartphones to government/app operators for digital contact tracing; precise GPS location is a departure
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: Measured appropriateness (5-point Likert, N=1,708, weighted Flanders sample, April 2020): GSM M=3.38 (SD=1.41), Bluetooth M=3.16 (SD=1.50), GPS M=2.99 (SD=1.55); GSM vs GPS t(1707)=17.196, p<.001, d=0.26; H1a confirmed — respondents differentiate significantly between data types, with precise GPS deemed least appropriate
departures: use of precise GPS location data (least appropriate of the three data types)
continuing any of these data flows after the pandemic ends (all data types drop below or near the scale midpoint post-COVID)
s5_norms.evidence: §4 Results (data-type comparisons, during COVID); means near the scale midpoint with SDs ~1.4-1.5 indicate substantial disagreement across respondents

s5_norms.norm_flow: During the pandemic, contact tracing data may be processed for the societal goal of estimating the spread of the virus, and (more weakly) for low-individual-impact goals such as suggesting a 14-day quarantine; processing for high-individual-impact goals such as limiting individuals' access to locations is a departure
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: Measured appropriateness during COVID: estimating spread M=3.77 (SD=1.37) > quarantine suggestion M=3.42 (SD=1.40) > limiting location access M=2.57 (SD=1.47); the societal vs high-impact contrast is very large (d=1.62); H2a confirmed — goals with high individual impact are rated less appropriate than societal ones
departures: using contact tracing data to limit individuals' access to certain locations (M=2.57, below the scale midpoint)
pursuing any of these goals after the pandemic ends
s5_norms.evidence: §4 Results (goal comparisons, during COVID); §5 Discussion (high-impact individual goals perceived as far less appropriate than low-impact suggestions or societal estimation)

s5_norms.norm_flow: The same contact tracing flows (all data types, all goals) continuing after the COVID-19 pandemic
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: Respondents anticipate significantly lower appropriateness post-pandemic for every data type and goal: GPS 2.99→2.54 (d=0.30), Bluetooth 3.16→2.65 (d=0.24), GSM 3.38→2.98 (d=0.28); limiting access 2.57→2.21 (d=0.25), quarantine suggestion 3.42→3.06 (d=0.26), estimating spread 3.77→3.51 (d=0.19); H3a and H3b confirmed — the informational norms are crisis-bound and time-sensitive
departures: treating pandemic-era acceptance as a stable post-crisis norm ('temporary measures established during a crisis become permanent and reduce citizens' privacy')
s5_norms.evidence: §4 Results (during vs after comparisons); §2.3.3 (normative transformation: 'norms are constantly in the process of becoming'); §5 Discussion (temporal element and mission-creep concern)
